title: POC performance standup - NyxLogic lab results
summary: Weekly POC sync to review lab benchmark delta vs incumbent, triage high tail latency, evaluate routing/fallback, and agree next steps for dedicated slot request and runbook.
next_steps: Redwood send tuned batching config and quantization test plan by 2027-07-10
NyxLogic provide 3 failing trace logs for 99p spikes by 2027-07-09
Schedule dedicated-slot provisioning call if lab delta persists by 2027-07-12
action_items: Avery: attach pricing + dedicated slot T&Cs by 2027-07-10
Diego: run quantize-8 test with 512-seqlen and share results by 2027-07-09
Tom: upload system logs/traces for 3 high-latency requests by 2027-07-09
header:
Date: 2027-07-08
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Marquez (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (NyxLogic Head of ML), Tom Richman (NyxLogic Platform Eng), Sara Li (NyxLogic CTO)
Recording: Yes
transcript:
[00:00] Avery: Hey everyone, good to see you, thanks for making time. Quick roll call, we have Diego and myself from Redwood.
[00:15] Maya: Hey, yes, Maya here.
[00:20] Tom: Tom on the call.
[00:23] Sara: Sara as well. Sorry, joined a minute late.
[00:30] Avery: No worries. This is our week-seven POC standup, we're focusing on the lab numbers vs your incumbent. We'll run through the slides but mostly show the numbers Diego pulled.
[00:42] Diego: Cool. I pushed the latest bench deck to the shared drive — link in the chat — and there's a short CSV with per-model shakes. Note: tests were run with batch sizes 1,2,4 and continuous batching on for the dedicated lanes.
[01:05] Maya: Quick question, were the baseline runs done on the same input distribution as our traffic? We had some differences last week.
[01:12] Diego: Good call. We reused the replay from Monday — same sequences and prompt mix — but we artificially injected a 25% long prompt tail to stress the 99th. Not identical but intentionally heavier tail.
[01:25] Tom: That explains the tail, yep.
[01:27] Sara: Ok. Show me numbers.
[01:32] Diego: Slide 3: median latency we at 42ms per token vs incumbent 58ms — so median delta looks good ~ -27%. However 99p we saw spikes to 1.2s vs incumbent 0.9s, so higher tail.
[02:00] Maya: Huh — so medians are better but we lose at tail, weird. Is that from batching or KV cache misses?
[02:10] Diego: Mostly KV cache thrash on long context windows, the way our cache keying interacts with your prompt prefixes. We saw cold-kv events when the prefix changed. Also an edge with our continuous batching that groups heterogeneous seq lengths causing small stragglers.
[02:35] Avery: To clarify, when you say KV cache thrash you mean repeated cache misses for similar prefixes?
[02:40] Diego: Exactly. The system is correct, it's just cross-request prefix variance; our cache eviction policy is LRU tied to session ID. When you have many short sessions with similar but not identical prefixes, you get churn.
[03:00] Tom: Could we pin session IDs on the client side to reduce churn? We've been rotating IDs for multi-tenant reasons.
[03:07] Maya: We rotate for privacy but maybe we can sticky for inference only — maybe tokenize differently.
[03:15] Diego: One option: prefix normalization on the client to reduce variance, or use our per-customer cache pinning for dedicated lanes. That requires dedicated slot to guarantee pin residency.
[03:30] Sara: That would push us toward dedicated. Is the cost delta big?
[03:35] Avery: We'll send a cost delta but short answer: dedicated improves tail and predictability, cost per-token is usually lower under steady throughput — but there's a monthly reservation fee.
[03:50] Diego: Back to numbers — throughput: on 4xA100-ish config we hit sustained 220 req/s for your 512 token average when batching=4; incumbent was 180 req/s. But throughput plateaus as sequence length >1024.
[04:12] Maya: So throughput better under average but not under long sequences, is that right?
[04:18] Diego: Yes. Quantization helps reduce per-token compute so it lowers median and throughput floor, but sometimes increases variance if kernels aren't stable.
[04:30] Tom: Did you test 8-bit quant with our model?
[04:34] Diego: We ran quantize-8 on 3 variants — q8_{naive}, q8_opt, and q4hf for reference. q8_opt gave a 15% median improvement and negligible quality regressions on our eval set, but 99p had mixed results.
[04:55] Maya: Mixed how — worse tail?
[04:58] Diego: Occasional 99p spikes due to some fallback paths using slower FP kernels when certain attention patterns show up. We think it's a kernel selection jitter.
[05:12] Sara: Can you force a stable kernel selection?
[05:16] Diego: There's a compilation knob we can set to favor deterministic kernels at the cost of small median perf. We'll run a compile with deterministic selection next run.
[05:28] Avery: Ok, so action: Diego to run quantize-8 with deterministic kernels.
[05:33] Diego: Yup, target to have results by Friday.
[05:37] [06:00] Maya: Another major point: are the error counts going up when you see 99p spikes? We had a few production errors last week.
[06:10] Diego: Error rates remain low, but we saw timeouts on the client when the 99p spiked which counted as errors on your side. Redwood retries are conservative, but you can configure tail timeouts.
[06:30] Tom: We're using a 1.5s request timeout for user-facing flows — maybe we need to bump for long form generation.
[06:36] Avery: We can recommend route-specific timeouts; our SDK supports per-route timeouts and circuit-breakers.
[06:45] Maya: Also curious about the routing/fallback playbook — you mentioned automatic fallback to smaller models when latency climbs?
[06:52] Diego: Yes, the smart routing policy can route to a smaller compatible model variant under SLO violations. But that requires co-deploying a lighter model and configuring similarity thresholds.
[07:05] Sara: If we fallback to smaller model, does output quality degrade noticeably?
[07:10] Diego: Slightly for some prompts. We can run A/B thresholds and automatic evaluation to keep degradation under a configured delta.
[07:20] Maya: Ok, we want fallback but with guardrails.
[07:24] Avery: We'll share a fallback config template.
[07:28] Diego: Quick note on network: we observed occasional egress bursts from your VPC that correlated to 99p events — might be periodic log upload. Could be network contention.
[07:42] Tom: That's interesting — we'll check our-side cron jobs and the ELB logs.
[07:46] [08:00] Maya: On benchmarks: can you explain the 'incumbent baseline' setup? They run on CloudVendorX managed endpoints with xGPU and their own prefix caching.
[08:12] Diego: We matched instance class but not the vendor's secret micro-ops. We also instrumented slightly different autogrowth. The important part is relative delta not absolute parity.
[08:25] Maya: Understood. We need parity tests eventually.
[08:28] Avery: For parity we can run side-by-side replay in your environment — we need temporary credentials for CloudVendorX read-only so we can replay from the same network path.
[08:40] Sara: Legal will push back on extra credentials. Can you do a replay using exported traces instead?
[08:46] Diego: Yes, traced replay is fine; we used that earlier. If you can export the trace and the payloads (redacted), we can replay in our lab.
[08:57] Tom: Ok we'll assemble a sanitized trace set.
[09:00] [09:30] Diego: Moving on — I wanted to highlight a weird outlier: a spike pattern correlated with requests that include JSON-ld style metadata at the top. The tokenizer expands a lot and that triggers KV churn.
[09:50] Maya: I think that's coming from a preamble Ak
[09:52] Maya: — yeah we add provenance block.
[09:55] Diego: If you can normalize or truncate or switch to hashed provenance, we reduce tokenization variance.
[10:05] Tom: That seems doable for non-critical fields. We'll try.
[10:10] [11:00] Avery: Any security or compliance blockers for the next steps?
[11:08] Sara: SOC2 is fine, but we need KMS integration for dedicated. Also audit log retention must be 1 year.
[11:15] Diego: Redwood Private supports KMS/HSM integrations; dedicated can be deployed in VPC with customer KMS. We'll send the SOC2 and KMS docs.
[11:25] Maya: Great. Send to legal inbox.
[11:28] [12:00] Diego: A quick demo of a run — I can share my screen but I'll dump the key numbers: 99p spikes correlate with cache eviction events at timestamps we annotated in the CSV. There's a clear pattern when multiple sessions rotate prefixes.
[12:45] Maya: These look convincing.
[12:48] Tom: For the dedicated slot ask, what's the minimum capacity to see tail improvement?
[12:55] Diego: Our tests show a single dedicated 8-GPU pool with pinning reduced 99p from 1.2s to 620ms for your workload. If you want headroom we'd recommend 12 GPUs for peak.
[13:15] Sara: Cost ballpark?
[13:18] Avery: We'll send estimate — conservative approx $XXk/month for 8 GPUs in reserved commit, discounts apply.
[13:28] Maya: Ok. Also, Diego, you mentioned a compile knob for deterministic kernels — how much median perf do we lose?
[13:35] Diego: About 6-8% median, but 99p tightens significantly — we saw reductions to 30-40% lower tail in internal tests.
[13:50] Tom: That tradeoff seems fine for user-facing flows.
[13:54] [15:00] Maya: One more: does Redwood support sample-level logging for evals? We need to compare outputs post-fallback.
[15:07] Diego: Yes, you can enable sample-level logging and redaction; it's opt-in on routes. There's a small throughput cost.
[15:20] Maya: Fine. We'll enable for 10k requests.
[15:24] Avery: Good. Next — any blockers to the next bench run?
[15:30] Tom: We'll prepare trace exports and check cron jobs.
[15:34] Sara: And we'll review legal for credentials.
[15:36] [16:00] Diego: I'll outline the test matrix: quantize-8 deterministic, compile tweaks, per-customer cache pinning, route timeouts bump to 2.5s, and replay.
[16:15] Maya: Sounds comprehensive.
[16:18] Avery: Recap and next steps: we'll run the quantization with deterministic kernels and share results by Friday; NyxLogic to send traces by Thursday; Redwood to send cost delta and dedicated slot T&Cs by next Monday.
[16:34] Tom: One tiny nit: can we get a CSV of per-request latencies rather than just percentiles? It helps our SRE.
[16:40] Diego: Yep I'll include per-request CSVs (sampled to 1%) to keep size reasonable.
[16:48] Maya: Anything else?
[16:51] Sara: No, thanks.
[16:53] Avery: Thanks all, we'll follow up in email and update the ticket.
[16:58] Maya: Thanks.
[17:00] Tom: Bye.
[17:02] (call ends)
